implementation_notes: .NET ships the assertion builder as first-party packages: JsonWebTokenHandler.CreateToken(SecurityTokenDescriptor) is the whole pattern, with Issuer, Audience/Audiences, Expires/IssuedAt/NotBefore, Claims or a ClaimsIdentity Subject, SigningCredentials and AdditionalHeaderClaims supplying the content, and the handler serializing and signing it into a compact JWS; the older System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt.JwtSecurityTokenHandler is the legacy shape of the same API. What replaces the classic structure: the descriptor plus the handler replace a hand-written builder class, so what remains yours is a factory that fixes issuer, TTL and mandatory claims, plus key material from an X509Certificate2, SymmetricSecurityKey or KMS-backed key. The consumer side is the mirror image in the same package (JsonWebTokenHandler.ValidateToken with TokenValidationParameters), and in ASP.NET Core AddJwtBearer installs it, leaving only issuance to write.
pitfalls: Subject and Claims are merged rather than rejected: a claim present in both is silently overridden by the Claims entry, so duplicate names hide configuration mistakes.
SigningCredentials built from a certificate whose private key is not persisted can end up ephemeral on some hosts; after a restart the issuer signs with a key no consumer can match.
TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew widens the accepted validity window on the consuming side, so a five-minute token can be honoured well past its exp unless the skew is set deliberately.
JsonWebTokenHandler and JwtSecurityTokenHandler map claim types differently (short versus long names), so mixing them across issuer and consumer silently breaks claim lookups.
